title: Mandatory National Service
resolution: Resolved: The United States should require one year of national service for young adults.
summary: Should every young American spend a year serving the country, in the military or in civilian programs like AmeriCorps?

background.p: The United States has had no military draft since 1973; young men must still register with the Selective Service System. Civilian service programs such as AmeriCorps and the Peace Corps are voluntary and pay modest living allowances. Several countries require military or civilian service, including Israel, South Korea, Switzerland and Norway, with very different rules.

In 2020, the congressionally created National Commission on Military, National, and Public Service released its final report, *Inspired to Serve*. It envisioned five million Americans beginning military, national or public service each year by 2031, so that service becomes "the norm, rather than the exception," and made recommendations on expanding service opportunities and on Selective Service registration.

terms.def: Full-time work for the public good, such as tutoring, conservation or disaster relief, usually for a modest stipend.
A federal agency that funds national service programs in communities.
The federal agency that keeps a list of men eligible for a military draft.
A person who refuses military service for reasons of conscience.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: A year of service would bring Americans together and meet real needs.

args.claim: Service brings together Americans from different backgrounds.
args.warrant: Working side by side with people from other regions, incomes and views builds understanding that few other experiences provide.
args.evidence: Studies of AmeriCorps and military service on civic attitudes; the National Commission's report.
args.response: The negative answers that voluntary programs already do this for those who choose, and forced participation may breed resentment.

args.warrant: Schools, parks, disaster areas and elder care need help; a year of service from millions of young adults supplies it.
args.evidence: AmeriCorps program evaluations; reports of labor shortages in caregiving and tutoring.
args.response: The negative replies that untrained short-term workers may not fill skilled needs, and paid jobs would be displaced.

args.claim: Young people gain skills and direction.
args.warrant: A structured year teaches responsibility and job skills and gives time to choose a path before college or work.
args.evidence: Surveys of service-program alumni; gap-year research.
args.response: The negative argues that delaying college or work costs young people a year of earnings and progress.

args.claim: Citizenship includes duties as well as rights.
args.warrant: A democracy asks citizens to serve on juries and pay taxes; a year of service is a fair way to share responsibility for the common good.
args.evidence: The Commission's vision of service as a norm; comparisons with countries that require service.
args.response: The negative replies that compulsory labor is a much larger demand than jury duty.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Service should be encouraged and expanded, but not required.

args.claim: Requiring a year of work intrudes on personal liberty.
args.warrant: Forcing young adults to spend a year in assigned work overrides their own choices about school, work and family.
args.evidence: Constitutional and philosophical debates about compulsory service; the history of opposition to the draft.
args.response: The affirmative answers that a wide menu of service options preserves choice within the requirement.

args.warrant: Millions of young adults a year need pay, housing, training and supervision, costing far more than current programs.
args.evidence: AmeriCorps cost-per-member figures multiplied by the size of an age group.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the work produced has real value, offsetting much of the cost.

args.warrant: People who choose to serve are motivated; expanding funded voluntary programs captures most of the benefits without compulsion.
args.evidence: The Commission's recommendations focused on expanding service opportunities; AmeriCorps waitlists.
args.response: The affirmative argues voluntary programs mostly attract people who are already civic-minded, missing the mixing that makes service valuable.

args.warrant: A required year postpones college and work, costing earnings and momentum, especially for students who are ready to start.
args.evidence: Research on delayed college entry and lifetime earnings.
args.response: The affirmative replies that many students benefit from a gap year, and service can include education benefits.

strawmen.strawman: They want to bring back the draft and send everyone to war.
strawmen.why: Most proposals include civilian options like tutoring and conservation.
strawmen.steelman: A year of military or civilian service would bring Americans together, meet real needs, and teach young people skills and citizenship.

strawmen.strawman: They think young people should only care about themselves.
strawmen.why: Many opponents support service, but voluntarily.
strawmen.steelman: Service should be expanded and encouraged, but requiring a year intrudes on liberty, costs enormously, and voluntary service captures most of the benefits.

weak.arg: Young people today are lazy and need discipline.
weak.why: An insult, not an argument, and it alienates judges.
An extreme comparison that minimizes real slavery and loses the judge.
